name: Beetroot juice

lead: Beetroot juice (BRJ) is a food-based supplement that contains high concentrations of inorganic nitrate, which the body converts to nitric oxide. Nitric oxide widens blood vessels, which lowers blood pressure and improves oxygen and nutrient delivery to tissues, including muscle.[1]

For looks, the chain runs through training: better blood flow and exercise tolerance can mean harder or longer sessions and a stronger pump, which supports muscle building and conditioning. Reviews of sports supplements list nitrates among the better-supported ergogenic aids, alongside creatine, beta-alanine, caffeine and protein.[2][13]

paras: It is drunk as juice or as concentrated shots, usually a couple of hours before exercise, and sometimes taken for several days beforehand. Athletes combine it with other pre-workout supplements. Effects are typically described over the hours after a drink and accumulate with several days of use.[8][11]

Common effects are red urine or stools (beeturia). Because nitrate lowers blood pressure, meta-analysis of hypertensive adults found a clinical systolic drop of about 5 mmHg,[5] which people on antihypertensives may want to discuss with a clinician. Reviews also note benefits and risks of regular use.[1]

chain: Dietary nitrate converts to nitric oxide
Blood vessels widen, oxygen delivery and muscle efficiency improve
Better endurance and recovery, more total training
angle.text: People drink it before workouts for pump and stamina. The look payoff comes from being able to train harder or longer, which over time supports muscle and conditioning.

lead: Beetroot juice is the pressed juice of red beets, a dietary source of inorganic nitrate. After drinking it, oral bacteria convert nitrate to nitrite and then nitric oxide, which dilates blood vessels, lowers blood pressure and may improve oxygen delivery and muscle efficiency.[1][2][3] The red pigment betanin is excreted largely unchanged, which can turn urine or stools pink or red (beeturia).[4]

In fitness circles it is used as a natural pre-workout. The appearance link runs through training: improved endurance, reduced fatigue, more repetitions before failure and better training performance can allow more work in the gym, which supports muscle gain and leanness over months.[2][5][6] Fitness writers also promote it for the muscle "pump", the temporary swelling of working muscle that they attribute to nitric oxide-driven blood flow.[7] A 2024 review of top sport supplements includes nitrates among those with the most robust evidence of efficacy and safety.[8]

Research on nitrate and beetroot juice dates to the late 2000s, when University of Exeter groups reported lower oxygen cost of exercise after nitrate loading.[3][9] It now includes dose-response work in healthy men,[10] reviews of cardiorespiratory endurance in athletes,[2] meta-analyses of resistance-exercise performance and muscle power,[6][11] and a 2025 umbrella review of physical performance in athletes and healthy individuals.[12]
infobox: Inorganic nitrate (beetroot juice also contains betanin pigment)[4]
Nitrate to nitrite to nitric oxide[1][3]
Plasma nitrite peaks about 2 to 3 hours after ingestion[3][13]

paras: Athletes use beetroot juice to improve endurance, and bodybuilders and gym-goers use it as a pump and pre-workout aid. Reviews report that nitric oxide increases blood flow, gas exchange and the efficiency of muscle contraction, which suggests ergogenic effects on cardiorespiratory endurance.[2]

Fitness-media articles describe it as a natural pre-workout: one August 2024 article defines the pump as temporary muscle swelling caused by increased blood flow and fluid accumulation and says nitric oxide is its key driver; it also lists reduced oxygen demand and lower soreness among claimed benefits, though without citing trials for several of those claims.[7] The Australian Institute of Sport lists dietary nitrate and beetroot juice among its performance supplements and says endurance, sprint and team-sport athletes have shown gains in exercise economy and capacity.[13]

A meta-analysis of 11 trials in 349 hypertensive adults found beetroot juice lowered clinical systolic blood pressure by 5.31 mmHg compared with controls, with moderate heterogeneity.[14] A systematic review notes possible applications in cardiovascular disease prevention.[1]

Nitrate was long regarded as an undesirable food component because of the possible formation of nitrosamines, though a 2015 review calls the evidence that it causes cancer weak and notes that nitrate has since been linked to physiological benefits.[3] In 2007 Larsen and colleagues reported that three days of sodium nitrate supplementation lowered oxygen uptake by about 3 to 5 percent during submaximal cycling.[3][9]

In 2009 Bailey and colleagues used beetroot juice as the nitrate source for the first time; across days 3 to 6 of a six-day period they observed roughly 5 percent lower oxygen uptake during low-intensity cycling and a 16 percent longer tolerable duration of high-intensity exercise.[3] Later studies used nitrate-depleted beetroot juice as a placebo, which did not improve economy or performance, suggesting that nitrate itself, rather than antioxidants or polyphenols alone, accounts for the effect.[3][9] Research then moved from acute dosing to multi-day protocols and to performance tests such as time trials, and the Exeter group's Andrew Jones summarised the field in a 2014 review.[9] Beetroot itself is an ancient crop, recorded in Babylonia in the 8th century BC and used in medieval Europe for digestive and blood-related ailments.[4]

A dose-response trial in 10 healthy men tested 70, 140 and 280 ml concentrated juice and examined plasma nitrite, blood pressure and exercise responses.[10] A randomized trial in trained soccer players reported better high-intensity intermittent performance after supplementation.[15] A 2018 review examined intermittent high-intensity efforts,[16] and a systematic review in elite soccer players described the evidence for dietary supplements generally as contradictory or scarce.[17]

Jones's 2014 review concluded that performance benefits are most consistent for roughly 5 to 30 minutes of high-intensity exercise, that several studies in highly trained endurance athletes found no benefit, and that individual responses vary; it was published in a supplement sponsored by the Gatorade Sports Science Institute.[9] The Australian Institute of Sport likewise notes that highly trained endurance athletes appear to gain little and that few studies have examined female athletes.[13]

A 2025 crossover trial in physically active people reported enhanced strength, reduced fatigue and improved recovery after short-term supplementation.[5] A combat-sports meta-analysis and a 2024 trial in female athletes also covered nitrate supplementation.[18][19]

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of six studies (about 92 resistance-trained men) found improvements in repetitions to failure (SMD about 0.43) and mean power in back squat and bench press, with no overall effect on peak power or peak velocity; the authors called the findings preliminary and noted small samples, varied placebos and that only one study verified nitrate dose.[6] A 2021 individual participant data meta-analysis of 19 double-blind crossover studies (268 participants) concluded that dietary nitrate increased maximal muscle power by about 5 percent, with a larger effect after a single acute dose than after multi-day dosing; the same authors note that meta-analyses show only a trivial effect on maximal strength.[11]
A pilot trial in adults with long COVID found changes in gut microbiota and inflammation but no improvement in functional outcomes.[20]

A systematic review summarizes benefits and risks of beetroot juice consumption.[1] The most recognized effects are beeturia and blood pressure lowering.[1][14] Beeturia, a pink or red tint to urine or stools from betanin, is described as harmless but can be mistaken for blood.[4] The Australian Institute of Sport also lists mild gastrointestinal discomfort, particularly with concentrated products, and states that antibacterial mouthwash can reduce conversion of nitrate to nitric oxide.[13]

Nitrate from vegetables is considered unlikely to be harmful according to expert views cited by Jones, though long-term effects of high-nitrate supplement use are not well studied; nitrite and nitrate salts carry risks of dosing errors and toxicity, including methemoglobinaemia, and the AIS advises against using them as supplements.[9][13]

Dietary nitrate raises plasma nitrite, which is reduced to nitric oxide, a vasodilator that increases oxygen and nutrient delivery to organs and muscle efficiency.[1][10] Oral bacteria on the tongue reduce nitrate to nitrite, which stomach acid and low-oxygen, low-pH tissue can convert to nitric oxide; plasma nitrite peaks about 2 to 3 hours after ingestion and nitrate returns to baseline after roughly 24 hours.[3] The juice used in the dose-response study contained about 5 to 8 mmol nitrate per serving.[10]

Proposed muscle effects include improved mitochondrial efficiency (a higher P/O ratio), sparing of phosphocreatine, better calcium handling and contractile function in fast-twitch fibres, and greater blood flow to type II fibres, with several of these shown in animal or small human studies.[3][9] Affourtit and colleagues note that it remains unproven whether nitric oxide itself mediates the effects and that nitrite can signal independently.[3]

Beetroot juice is sold as juice, concentrated shots and powders and is marketed as a pre-workout. The Australian Institute of Sport notes that few commercial products have been independently tested for nitrate content and that beetroot concentrates are preferred over many marketed products.[13] Online fitness articles recommend taking about 500 ml of juice an hour or two before training, and some describe taking it for several days beforehand; these articles often do not cite trials for their pump and recovery claims.[7]

Randomized and crossover trials cover soccer players,[15] physically active adults,[5] female athletes[19] and healthy men,[10] with reviews synthesizing endurance[2] and overall performance results,[12] and meta-analyses of resistance exercise and muscle power.[6][11] A 2018 Circulation Research editorial commented on a trial of beetroot juice in a randomized setting.[21] Results vary by population and training level across the literature.

lore.intro: In gym and bodybuilding communities beetroot juice is discussed as a natural alternative to synthetic pre-workouts, valued for pump and stamina; much of the popular writing is by fitness media rather than researchers.[7]

claims.claim: Beetroot juice gives a bigger muscle pump.
It lets you do more reps and train harder.
It improves endurance and lowers the oxygen cost of exercise.
It speeds recovery and reduces soreness.
Home-juiced beets are as good as commercial shots.
Antibacterial mouthwash can blunt the effect.
